subject: Maths
title: Discriminant
subtitle: Quadratic Equations · GCSE Maths
learning_objective: I can use the discriminant to determine the number and nature of roots of a quadratic equation.

key_vocab.definition: The discriminant of ax² + bx + c = 0 is b² − 4ac. It tells us how many real roots (solutions) the quadratic has.

sections.title: Learning Objective
sections.content: I can use the discriminant to determine the number and nature of roots of a quadratic equation.

sections.title: Key Words
sections.content: discriminant -- The discriminant of ax² + bx + c = 0 is b² − 4ac. It tells us how many real roots (solutions) the quadratic has.

sections.title: Method
sections.content:
The discriminant b² − 4ac determines the nature of roots: positive = 2 roots, zero = 1, negative = none.
Δ = b² − 4ac
Δ > 0: two roots; Δ = 0: one root; Δ < 0: no real roots

Key examples:
  ✓ x² + 5x + 6: b²−4ac = 25−24 = 1 > 0, two roots  (positive discriminant)
  ✓ x² − 6x + 9: b²−4ac = 36−36 = 0, one root  (zero discriminant)
  ✓ x² + x + 1: b²−4ac = 1−4 = −3 < 0, no real roots  (negative discriminant)
  ✗ Discriminant = b² + 4ac  (must be b² MINUS 4ac)
  ✗ b² − 4ac < 0 means two real roots  (negative means no real roots)

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Example 1 – two real roots
  Find the discriminant of x² + 3x − 10 = 0 and state the number of roots.
  a = 1, b = 3, c = −10
  Δ = 3² − 4(1)(−10) = 9 + 40 = 49
  Δ = 49 > 0, so two distinct real roots
  Two distinct real roots
  (Since 49 is a perfect square, the roots will be rational.)

Example 2 – repeated root
  Find the discriminant of x² − 8x + 16 = 0.
  a = 1, b = −8, c = 16
  Δ = (−8)² − 4(1)(16) = 64 − 64 = 0
  Δ = 0, so one repeated root
  One repeated root
  (The quadratic is a perfect square: (x − 4)² = 0.)

sections.title: Calculating the discriminant
sections.content:
Find b² − 4ac for each equation.

(a) x² + 5x + 6 = 0
(b) x² − 4x + 4 = 0
(c) 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0
(d) x² + 2x + 5 = 0

sections.title: Stating number of roots
sections.content:
Find the discriminant and state the number of real roots.

(a) x² + 7x + 10 = 0
(b) x² − 6x + 9 = 0
(c) x² + x + 1 = 0
(d) 3x² − 2x − 1 = 0

sections.title: Proving no real roots
sections.content:
Show each equation has no real roots.

(a) x² + 4x + 5 = 0
(b) 2x² + x + 1 = 0
(c) 3x² − x + 2 = 0
(d) x² + 6x + 10 = 0

sections.title: Finding parameters
sections.content:
Find the value(s) of k for the stated condition.

(a) x² + kx + 4 = 0, equal roots
(b) x² − 6x + k = 0, equal roots
(c) kx² + 2x + 1 = 0, equal roots (k ≠ 0)
(d) x² + 4x + k = 0, no real roots

sections.title: Mixed discriminant problems
sections.content:
Use the discriminant to answer each question.

(a) Does x² + 3x + 1 = 0 have real roots?
(b) For what values of p does x² + px + 25 = 0 have one root?
(c) Show 5x² − 3x + 1 = 0 has no real solutions.
(d) Find k if 2x² + kx + 8 = 0 has equal roots.
(e) Does 4x² − 12x + 9 = 0 have one or two roots?

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
✓ b² − 4ac = 0 means one repeated root
✗ The discriminant is b² + 4ac
✓ A negative discriminant means no real roots
✗ b² − 4ac > 0 means no roots
✓ If Δ is a perfect square, the roots are rational

teacher_sections.title: Teacher Key & Mark Scheme
teacher_sections.content:
Award marks for correct working and final answers.

Calculating the discriminant:
  (a) 1
  (b) 0
  (c) 49
  (d) −16

Stating number of roots:
  (a) Δ = 9 > 0; two roots
  (b) Δ = 0; one root
  (c) Δ = −3 < 0; no real roots
  (d) Δ = 16 > 0; two roots

Proving no real roots:
  (a) Δ = 16 − 20 = −4 < 0
  (b) Δ = 1 − 8 = −7 < 0
  (c) Δ = 1 − 24 = −23 < 0
  (d) Δ = 36 − 40 = −4 < 0

Finding parameters:
  (a) k = ±4
  (b) k = 9
  (c) k = 1
  (d) k > 4

Mixed discriminant problems:
  (a) Δ = 5 > 0; yes, two
  (b) p = ±10
  (c) Δ = 9 − 20 = −11 < 0
  (d) k = ±8
  (e) Δ = 144 − 144 = 0; one root
